{"slots": {"question": [{"claim": "Whether the use of stigmatizing labels like 'convicted criminal' in political advertisements against figures like Donald Trump causes a spillover effect that negatively impacts broader public perceptions of all individuals with criminal records.", "quotes": [{"text": "To test for the possibility of stigmatizing language spillover, this preliminary study employs a survey experiment testing exposure to the Party’s advertisement, labeling Trump as a “convicted criminal” (n = 814) relative to no advertisement (n = 813), on Democrats’ perceptions of individuals with records and several dimensions of perceived representation.", "page": 1}]}],
"central_claim": [{"claim": "Exposure to political advertisements using stigmatizing labels for Trump negatively affects Democrats' perceptions of people with criminal records, but this negative effect can be mitigated by providing a counter-stereotype through perspective-getting.", "quotes": [{"text": "Results suggest that exposure to the Trump advertisement with the “convicted criminal” label had significant, negative impacts on Democrats’ perceptions of individuals with records, but improved perceived feelings of representation.", "page": 1}, {"text": "Findings suggest that the counter-stereotype vastly ameliorated the negative effects of the advertisement on Democrats’ perceptions of individuals with criminal records.", "page": 1}]}],
"evidence": [{"claim": "The study used a survey experiment with 2,439 self-identified Democrats in the United States, randomized into three groups: a control group, a group exposed to a Trump advertisement labeled 'CONVICTED CRIMINAL', and a group exposed to a counter-narrative about a formerly system-involved state representative before the advertisement.", "quotes": [{"text": "the 2,439 participants were allocated approximately evenly across one of three different treatment groups: a) the Control group (n = 813); b) the Trump Ad Alone group (n = 814); and c) the Counter-Narrative First group (n = 812).", "page": 4}]}],
"key_findings": [{"claim": "The Trump advertisement alone, which uses the label 'convicted criminal,' significantly decreases positive perceptions of individuals with criminal records and increases perceived self-interest motives of elected officials.", "quotes": [{"text": "exposure to the Trump advertisement alone significantly decreased (positive) perceptions of individuals with criminal records ( β̂0 = −0.835, SE = 0.044) and significantly increased participants beliefs that elected officials’ motivations were to serve the public, versus serving their own self-interest ( β̂0 = 0.130, SE = 0.049).", "page": 11}]}],
{"claim": "Providing a counter-narrative via perspective-getting significantly increases positive perceptions of individuals with criminal records compared to seeing the advertisement alone.", "quotes": [{"text": "exposure to the counter-narrative prior to being presented with the Trump advertisement increased positive perceptions of individuals with criminal records by more than 0.8 standard deviation (SD) units, compared to those presented with the Trump advertisement alone", "page": 11}]}],
{"claim": "A counter-narrative describing a public-service-oriented person with a criminal record significantly reduces support for using stigmatizing political advertisements.", "quotes": [{"text": "exposure to the counter-narrative significantly decreased support for the Trump advertisement, relative to the Trump advertisement alone ( β̂2 = −0.172 SE = 0.048).", "page": 11}]}],
{"claim": "The negative impacts of the Trump advertisement on perceptions of individuals with criminal records were almost entirely neutralized when a counter-narrative was presented first.", "quotes": [{"text": "the strength of the counter-narrative is not unexpected, but promising... these effects were almost entirely ameliorated ( β̂2 = 0.833, whereas β̂0 = −0.835).", "page": 15}]}],
"scope_and_limits": [{"claim": "The study is a preliminary survey experiment and requires field experiments to confirm findings, and it did not use a full factorial design, meaning it cannot isolate the effect of the counter-narrative alone from its combination with the advertisement.", "quotes": [{"text": "While well-powered and aptly-timed field experiments are needed to confirm and extend these findings", "page": 1}, {"text": "the decision on which arm to drop was entirely intentional based on the priority research questions... the counter-narrative arm cannot be directly compared to the pure control arm to test the impact of the counter-narrative alone because it also involves exposure to the Trump advertisement.", "page": 10}]}],
"theoretical_positioning": [{"claim": "The paper applies social categorization theory, specifically regarding category salience and group exemplars, to predict that stigmatizing labels applied to a prominent figure will spill over to the broader group.", "quotes": [{"text": "Leaning upon social categorization theory, propagating such labels on Trump may thereby spillover, impacting constituents’ perspectives of individuals with records more broadly.", "page": 1}]}],
"interlocutor_claim": [{"claim": "The author notes that prior evidence suggests negative campaign advertisements are often used less by those leading in polls, while Democrats tend to respond more to positive ads.", "quotes": [{"text": "prior evidence on the effects of negative campaign advertisements suggests that they tend to be utilized less by those leading in the polls [4,5] and that Democrats tend to respond more to positive ads, compared to Republicans [6].", "page": 2}]}]}], "order_of_operations": "null"}
